sentences.text: This dinosaur could reach lengths of 5 to 6 meters and weigh between 454 and 907 kilograms.
Its skull measured approximately 30 centimeters in total length.
Ribs from specimens are strongly curved and thickened, measuring between 50 and 100 centimeters in length.
Like other ankylosaurids, it had heavy armor and a club on its tail, which limited its speed.
Although initially described with four digits, the animal likely had three toes on its feet, consistent with other ankylosaurids.
The preserved left foot was proven to be an artifact of the initial mount, confirming three digits were more probable.
The genus was described by Evgeny Maleev in 1952.
The first remains were discovered in 1948.
The species Talarurus plicatospineus was named by Maleev in 1952.
The wide, stocky rostrum suggests it was an efficient grazer feeding on low vegetation in flat terrain.
It possessed a broad, rectangular snout adapted for grazing low vegetation.
Research suggests it was a grazer herbivore, while its contemporary Tsagantegia was a browser herbivore.
The fused, semi-rectangular maxilla was likely useful on flat surfaces.
Studies of the endocranial region indicate that ankylosaurids like this animal had well-developed gaze stabilization and auditory senses, unlike nodosaurids.
The flocculus, a brain structure related to balance, was first reported in this animal and is common in ankylosaurids but absent or reduced in nodosaurids.
Ankylosaurids like this animal possessed a large range of sound perception, particularly for low frequencies, based on their anatomy.
The elongated lagena indicates that ankylosaurs had a wide range of sound perception, particularly for low frequencies.
It is classified within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae of the family Ankylosauria.
Maleev originally assigned it to the family Syrmosauridae in 1952, which is now known as Ankylosauridae.
Recent phylogenetic analysis provides evidence for assigning it to Ankylosaurinae, a derived group of ankylosaurids.
It lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 96 to 89 million years ago.
It lived during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 96 to 89 million years ago.
This animal lived in what is now Asia during the Turonian stage of the mid-Cretaceous.
It lived from the Cenomanian to the Santonian stages, between 100.5 and 83.6 million years ago.
It is unclear whether slight differences in caputegulae on skull roof PIN 3780/1 represent a taxonomic issue, according to Arbour and Currie.
Walter Preston Coombs suggested it was the same species as Euoplocephalus, but later studies did not support this claim.
Most skeletal mounts are outdated due to numerous anatomical errors, such as ribs pointing downward instead of outward as seen in most ankylosaurids.
